Senses.Explanation: Inner succession is the inward side of the royal-line analogy used in Five-Ranks discourse. Jiufeng Daoqian defines it as knowing how to take responsibility within, distinguishes it from outer succession in the minister’s position, and still places the royal seed beyond both taking responsibility and carrying a burden. In Jiufeng Daoqian’s exchange, a questioner asks whether outward succession is the minister’s position and inward succession the royal seed. Jiufeng accepts the setup, then defines outer and inner succession separately before refusing to equate inner succession with the royal seed itself. The Records Pointing at the Moon and the Compendium of the Five Lamps preserve that same explicit definition, while the Complete Collection and Strict Lineage repeat the case in separate works. Hongzhi Zhengjue uses ‘inner succession arriving home’ opposite ‘branching off and borrowing the road’ in a public address. Yongjue Yuanxian distinguishes royal-prince Five Ranks as internally divided into inner and outer succession. The corpus therefore gives a technical relation, not a generic synonym for transmission.

Senses.Explanation: Oxherding pictures are illustrated and versified Chan sequences that arrange the ox-and-herder image into named stages; the corpus preserves more than one ten-picture order and also warns that diagrams can become stale goods. The Puming arrangement begins with the ox unherded, moves through initial restraint and habituation, and ends with both ox and herder forgotten. A second sequence runs from searching for the ox through finding traces, seeing and gaining it, returning home, forgetting ox and person, returning to the source, and entering the marketplace. Prefaces connect the pictures with older public ox-herding exchanges and invite readers to compare their own position. Yet Zhuhong's preface explicitly says that for someone who enters directly, the picture becomes stale merchandise and the verse surplus talk. Later prefaces likewise treat different arrangements and responses as material for examination, not an invariant prescription.

Senses.Explanation: Oxherding verses are an ordered Chan verse-sequence that stages seeking, finding, handling, losing, and moving beyond the ox. The label is not admitted from contents headings alone: complete sequences follow it in masters’ records, other masters write named harmonizations, and Yuetong publicly tests a request for such verses by saying that one must use one’s own. Jiguang Huo’s record prints the label directly before a staged sequence beginning with entering the hills to seek the ox and continuing through finding tracks, catching, tending, forgetting ox and person, returning to the source, and entering the marketplace. Shiyu Mingfang, Xiangtian Jinian Jingxian, and Fushi Tongxian each supply actual harmonized sequences rather than bare catalogue labels; their opening stage names and first lines are preserved beside the exact headword. The Brocade River lamp biography quotes an oxherding verse after saying its subject harmonized an earlier sequence. When Sanmu asks Yuetong for oxherding verses, Yuetong answers that one must use one’s own and then tests Sanmu’s attempted whisk gesture. The genre is therefore deployed inside an interview as well as transmitted in verse sections.

Senses.Explanation: A child who tends cattle: a herdboy, cowherd boy, or oxherd boy. The term is attested, and Chan records concentrate its distinctive use in oxherding songs, pictures, public questions, and verse. In Puming's ten oxherding verses, the boy holds the grass rope without slack and works all day; later, when there is no ox anywhere, the boy is idle, claps, sings under the moon, and still returns to “one further barrier.” Fenyang Shanzhao's Herdboy Song says that the boy does not copy texts or read a single graph, yet unfolds countless scrolls and handles question and answer. Asked “what is the herdboy's song?” Xuefeng Yicun dances and leaves the teaching hall. Jiashan Lingquan Ziying answers “who is the person within Jiashan's scene?” with “the herdboy sings in the open fields; the woodcutter laughs deep in the clouds.” Dizang Shouen, Danxia Zichun, Hongzhi Zhengjue, and Furong Daokai further place the boy in teaching-seat and portrait verse. Zen bends the ordinary cattle-tending child into a recurring actor in staged ox-and-herder sequences, direct interview answers, and teaching-seat songs; different stages of the same herdboy-and-ox use are not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: To look around is to turn and look at a person, direction, or assembly. The verb retains that visual sense in Emperor Suzong's complaint that Nanyang Huizhong does not look at him and in an unnamed monk's looking east and west for the absent Changqing Da'an. Chan records also make it a recurrent teaching-seat stage direction. At an opening of the hall Xuedou Chongxian “looked around at the assembly” (顧視大眾) before speaking; Yungai Zhiyong follows the look with a shout and questions concerning host and guest. In one encounter Mazu Daoyi merely looks, Yangshan Huiji comments on the look, and the exchange ends. Ciji Cong compresses speech and action still further: “then he looked around at the assembly and said, ‘stop!’” (乃顧視大眾曰休). Yulin Tongxiu looks left and right, strikes the staff, and leaves the seat (顧視左右，卓拄杖，下座). Thus an ordinary look is bent into an observable public-address action of the teaching seat; the entry does not assign the look an unspoken symbolic message.

The exact pair therefore names a transmitted procedure, not an incidental act of checking a mirror.

Senses.Explanation: The expression names Yunmen’s sequence: he looks toward the interlocutor, says “Look!”, and cuts off the attempted answer with “Hah!” Yunmen’s own record describes the interaction: he sometimes looked toward the recorded questioner and said “Look!”; when the questioner prepared to answer, Yunmen said “Hah!” The monasteries consequently named Yunmen by this look-and-two-utterance sequence. A collected transmission states the same sequence and adds that Deshan Yuanming later removed the initial look and called the shortened form “drawn look.” Later texts use the compact phrase as a named case, ask how it operates at face-to-face meeting, and place it alongside Yunmen’s other characteristic responses. The punctuation and speaker sequence matter: this is a recorded look and two utterances, not an abstract three-word maxim.
